journal.label: Design Note 01
journal.title: Learn by building, not only by watching
journal.excerpt: A project turns vague learning into specific questions.
journal.more: When I started learning Unreal Engine 5, I watched one or two introductory tutorials to understand the editor, then began a solo project. Building exposed the exact problems I needed to solve next. The lesson is not to avoid tutorials; it is to use them with a concrete purpose and apply what I learn immediately.

journal.label: Design Note 02
journal.title: A deadline is a scope tool
journal.excerpt: The Wrong Floor taught me to protect the central idea under time pressure.
journal.more: Approaching The Wrong Floor as a game-jam project helped turn a university assignment into a bounded production challenge. Under 72 hours, prioritization is part of the design: every additional feature takes time away from completing and polishing the experience.

journal.label: Design Note 03
journal.title: A vista gives the player a reason to move
journal.excerpt: Abandoned Temple was a short exercise in making the destination and route readable.
journal.more: The Abandoned Temple task required a clear vista and a golden path using supplied elements. The time limit made it useful to focus on the relationship between the focal point, the route, and what the player can understand from the space.

projects.title: Lab-1995
projects.tagline: An ongoing solo psychological-horror project developed while learning Unreal Engine 5 through hands-on production.
projects.challenge: Build an original game independently while learning the engine and making practical design and implementation decisions along the way.
projects.solution: Use the project itself as a learning framework: develop the game, identify gaps in knowledge, and apply new skills directly to the work.
projects.outcome: An ongoing Unreal Engine 5 project. The work and its systems continue to evolve.
lessons: Building a real project creates concrete questions that passive tutorial-watching cannot answer on its own.
Solo development requires balancing learning, implementation, and scope.

blocks.text: A solo project built by learning through making.

Lab-1995 is an ongoing psychological-horror game I am developing on my own in Unreal Engine 5. I have been learning the engine alongside development, using the project to turn new knowledge into working features rather than treating learning and production as separate phases.
The approach: learn what the project needs next.

Rather than waiting until I felt fully prepared, I began building and learned the tools and systems as the project demanded them. That approach makes each new topic immediately useful, while also exposing the trade-offs involved in making a game independently.

blocks.title: Learning through implementation
blocks.text: Each development problem gives me a specific question to investigate, test, and apply to the project.
blocks.takeaway: The project is both a game in development and a practical learning process.

blocks.text: Current status
Lab-1995 is still in development. This page will grow alongside the project, with additional breakdowns added as individual mechanics, levels, and implementation decisions are ready to document.

projects.results: Ongoing. The project demonstrates an end-to-end solo development process alongside learning Unreal Engine 5.

projects.title: The Wrong Floor
projects.tagline: A university project approached as a game jam—and completed in under 72 hours.
projects.challenge: Deliver a coherent playable horror experience within a very short time limit, without allowing scope to overwhelm the core idea.
projects.solution: Treat the assignment like a game jam: prioritize the central experience, make scope decisions quickly, and focus effort on what supports the main idea.
projects.outcome: Completed in under 72 hours. The project became an exercise in focused scope and rapid delivery.
lessons: A clear central idea makes time-limited decisions easier.
Finishing requires deciding what not to build.
A university brief can become a useful production constraint when treated as a delivery challenge.

blocks.text: One small project. One hard deadline.

The Wrong Floor began as a solo university project. I decided to approach it like a game jam and completed it in under 72 hours. The constraint forced me to focus on the essential experience instead of expanding the idea beyond what the available time could support.
Designing within the constraint

The main production challenge was deciding which parts of the experience deserved the limited time available. The approach was to protect the core concept, make decisions quickly, and avoid adding work that did not help deliver a complete project.

blocks.title: Scope is a design decision
blocks.text: Under a short deadline, every additional feature competes with finishing, testing, and polishing the central experience.
blocks.takeaway: The project was completed in under 72 hours.

blocks.heading: Selected visuals from The Wrong Floor

blocks.text: What this project demonstrates
The most useful takeaway is not simply speed; it is the ability to constrain a project, prioritize its central idea, and bring a solo project to completion under a strict deadline.

projects.contribution: Solo development under a strict deadline.
projects.team: Started as a solo university project and approached as a game-jam challenge.

projects.title: Four-Player Circular Chess
projects.tagline: A physical tabletop chess variant exploring how four-player movement and a circular board shape strategic choices.
projects.vision: Adapt the familiar strategic language of chess into a circular board where four players share the same space and must read threats from more than one direction.
projects.challenge: Create a board that is easy to read at a glance while giving four players distinct starting zones and enough space to understand movement and threats.
projects.solution: Designed a circular, color-coded board layout, documented the rules visually, and built a physical prototype with handmade pieces to make the concept tangible.
projects.outcome: A photographed physical prototype with a digital board layout, rule reference, and four color-coded sets of pieces. Further balancing and rule validation can be documented as the design develops.
lessons: Board readability matters: player zones, piece identity, and movement paths need to remain clear from different seating positions.
A physical prototype helps reveal practical issues of scale, contrast, piece handling, and table space earlier than a digital mock-up alone.

blocks.text: A familiar strategy game, rearranged around a shared centre.

Four-Player Circular Chess is a tabletop board-game design project built around a circular board and four color-coded player sides. The project combines a digital layout with a handmade physical prototype, including the board surface and individual pieces.
Design challenge

A circular layout changes how players scan the board. With four sides in play, the visual design needs to distinguish each player clearly and keep the centre, rings, and movement spaces legible without relying on a conventional rectangular grid.
From layout to physical prototype

I developed the board graphic, arranged the player zones, prepared a visual rules reference, and made the physical version by hand. The pieces were formed and painted in separate colors so each side could be identified quickly during setup.

blocks.title: Prototype-first design
blocks.text: The board and pieces are physical rather than just a screen mock-up, making scale, contrast, and handling part of the design process.
blocks.takeaway: A prototype is useful when it lets you inspect the real object players will use.

blocks.text: What I would validate next

The next useful step is structured playtesting: verify that the movement rules are understood consistently, check whether turns stay engaging with four players, and adjust the board or rules where players hesitate. I am keeping those as validation goals rather than claiming balance has already been proven.

projects.challenge: Create two levels for a railway simulator, with each level targeting a substantial 30–40 minute gameplay experience.

projects.title: Beyond Guilt
projects.tagline: A first-person judgment simulator where investigation, sentencing, and the state of Hell respond to the player’s choices.

banner.alt: Beyond Guilt courtroom concept image from the game design document

projects.duration: Ongoing · Demo and full release planned
projects.team: Solo developer; a university project being developed with commercial release as the intention.
projects.vision: Beyond Guilt is a first-person courtroom management game in which the player serves as the Judge of the Afterlife. Each day, five criminal souls stand trial; the player investigates, questions each soul, delivers a verdict, and assigns a punishment.
projects.challenge: Connect investigation and judgment with longer-term Hell management and changes in how future souls behave.
projects.solution: The GDD defines a cycle of reviewing Hell, investigating a case, questioning a soul, delivering a verdict, assigning punishment, and reviewing the day’s consequences. Planned systems include facility state, judge reputation, and soul adaptation.
projects.outcome: Ongoing Unity 6 (URP) project. The design document describes intended systems and plans; it does not by itself verify which systems are already implemented.
lessons: A case study should distinguish the designed experience from implemented and tested features.
The core loop connects individual moral decisions to longer-term simulation consequences.
projects.contribution: Solo development, game design, and implementation in Unity 6 (URP). Specific completed mechanics can be added as they are verified in the build.
projects.results: In development. The project is intended for commercial release; no release or playtest results are claimed here.

blocks.text: Every verdict changes more than one life.

Beyond Guilt is my ongoing solo project in Unity 6 (URP). It is also a university project, but I am developing it with the intention of releasing it commercially. The player takes the role of the Judge of the Afterlife, deciding the fate of criminal souls while managing the long-term state of Hell.
The daily gameplay loop

The design document describes each in-game day as five criminal cases. The player reviews Hell’s current condition, investigates evidence, questions a soul, delivers a verdict, assigns a punishment, and then reviews the consequences at the end of the day.
Four core design pillars

The GDD organizes the game around Investigation, Judgment, Hell Management, and Adaptive Souls. Investigation is about finding the truth; judgment asks the player to decide what is fair; Hell management makes sentencing affect the wider system; and adaptive souls are intended to respond to the Judge’s reputation and past decisions.

projects.title: Abandoned Temple
projects.tagline: A two-hour level-prototyping exercise focused on a clear vista and a readable golden path.

banner.alt: Top-down view of the Abandoned Temple level prototype with route annotations

projects.team: Individual level-prototyping task assigned by professor.
projects.contribution: Created a level from a given set of elements, with a clear vista and a golden path, within the two-hour time limit.
projects.results: Completed the prototype in under two hours. No playtest or usability outcome is claimed.
projects.vision: Create a readable temple level using the supplied elements, with a clear vista and a golden path.
projects.challenge: The brief was to assemble a level from the provided elements and make the intended route and visual destination legible.
projects.solution: Used the given environment pieces to shape a central space, a route through it, and a visible focal point. The top-down image includes route annotations that make the intended path easier to discuss.
projects.outcome: A level prototype completed in under two hours, documented with a top-down layout and a short gameplay video.
lessons: A clear vista can orient the player before they reach the destination.
A golden path should guide without making the space feel like a featureless corridor.
Time-boxed prototyping makes layout priorities and trade-offs visible.

blocks.text: A level prototype built in under two hours.

Abandoned Temple was a speed level-prototyping task assigned by my professor. The brief was to create a level from a supplied set of elements, with a clear vista and a golden path. I completed the prototype in under two hours.
Top-down route and composition

The top-down view documents the overall layout and intended player route. The annotated lines and crosses are part of the planning image, helping explain the path through the central area and the points where movement or sightlines were being considered.

blocks.alt: Top-down level layout with route annotations
blocks.caption: Top-down layout and pathing notes

blocks.text: Gameplay walkthrough

The short video shows the prototype from a player-facing perspective. It complements the top-down view: one communicates the layout, while the other helps communicate the experience of moving through the space.

blocks.title: The brief drove the layout
blocks.text: The goal was not to build a large finished environment. It was to use the supplied elements to establish a clear vista and a readable golden path under a strict time limit.
What this exercise demonstrates

This prototype is a compact example of level-design thinking under constraints: identify the focal point, arrange the route, and communicate the intended flow before investing in a larger production pass.
